newsitem.title: NORWAY: NORWAY ENDS SEARCH FOR SURVIVORS IN SHIP DISASTER.
newsitem.headline: NORWAY ENDS SEARCH FOR SURVIVORS IN SHIP DISASTER.

text.p: The Norwegian rescue service called off a fruitless search on Sunday for survivors from a Greek cargo ship which sank with its Polish crew of 20.
The Leros Strength, a 22,000 tonne bulk carrier, went down on Saturday about 30 miles west of the Norwegian North Sea port of Stavanger in waves six metres (20 feet) high.
An initial search yielded life vests, two life rafts and the ship's name plate, but no trace of the vessel itself or its crew following a disaster that put the spotlight on bulk carrier safety.
"The chances of finding any survivors now are nil," Anders Bang-Andersen, a rescue service spokesman in Stavanger, said after the operation was abandoned at noon (1100 GMT).
He said the 21-year-old bulk carrier, which Norwegian maritime authorities said had been in a poor condition, was lying in 258 metres of water.
Polish Baltic port of Gdynia went into mourning on Sunday as last hopes faded of rescuing the crew.
Festivities scheduled for Sunday and Monday to mark Gdynia's 71st anniversary have been cancelled and flags in the city have been draped with black ribbons.
Monday's anniversary session of the City Council would also have a mourning character, it added.
Nineteen of the crew were from Gdansk province which includes the city and 10 from Gdynia itself.
A statement by Gdynia's Maritime Agency said the crew had been insured, dispelling earlier reports that their families may have been left penniless after the disaster.
The ship went down apparently as the captain, identified by the Polish Ship Rescue service in Gdynia as Eugeniusz Arciszewski, was calling the Norwegian rescue service for help.

Norwegian officials said he reported a hole in the bow, that the ship was taking in water and that he had problems navigating. The line went dead after three minutes and the ship probably sank very quickly, the officials said.
Built in 1976, it was registered in Cyprus but owned by Greek shipping company Leros Management, they said.

The Norwegian news agency NTB quoted the Norwegian Maritime Directorate as saying the ship was held in the Dutch port of Rotterdam on August 13 last year because of 11 complaints about its condition. They included everything from insufficient rescue gear to faults in the navigational system, NTB said.
It said 559 sailors had died in disasters involving bulk carriers in the past five years around the world.
"Leros Strength's sinking is a dramatic confirmation that bulk carriers are not safe enough," NTB quoted Tore Hoeifoedt, spokesman for classificiation society Det Norske Veritas, as saying.
"Most bulk carrier accidents occur when water floods a cargo hold. If bulkheads are not watertight, the water will flow into the next hold and the ship will go under within seconds," he said.

New standards to reduce the risk of bulk carriers sinking as a result of their holds flooding were adopted last December by the International Association of Classification Societies. (IACS). Measures to reinforce bulkheads are to be phased in from July next year.
Leros Strength was carrying apatite, a crystalline mineral used in the manufacture of fertilisers, from Murmansk, Russia, to Poland.
It was the worst ship disaster off Norway for years.
